They may draw attention to conditions they want changed.

A bill must go through three readings in the Folketing before it can finally be passed.
The purpose is among other things to ensure that bills are thoroughly handled.
The third reading of the bill ends with a vote.
If there is a majority for the bill, it is passed.
If there is a majority against, it is rejected.

That means the politicians make the political decisions on behalf of the population.
In return, the politicians must answer to the voters on election day.
This representative democracy is sometimes supplemented by direct democracy in the form of referendums, folkeafstemninger.
Here the population takes part directly in the democratic decision process.
They can themselves decide whether they are for or against a specific bill.
The constitution lays down that some questions must be decided by a referendum.
That applies, among other things, if the constitution or the voting age is to be changed.
A minority of the Folketing's members of at least one third, that is 60 members, can also demand that a passed bill be put to the voters for approval or rejection.
There are also rules about a referendum when Denmark gives up its right of self-determination, its sovereignty, by taking part in international cooperation.

If fewer than 150 of the Folketing's 179 members, but still a simple majority of at least 90 members, have said yes to Denmark taking part in the international cooperation, a referendum is held on whether Denmark should take part.
This rule has become especially important in connection with Denmark's membership of the EU.
Since the constitution was last changed in 1953, 16 referendums have been held.
More than half of them have been about Denmark's relationship to the EU.

Democracy does not only live in Christiansborg.
Local self-government is a cornerstone of Danish democracy.
It has deep roots in history that local communities solve many of society's common tasks.
Denmark is among the countries in Europe that have placed the most tasks with local and regional government, in municipalities and regions.
The tasks of Danish municipalities in particular have grown strongly as the welfare society has developed.
Today municipalities and regions solve a wide range of the public sector's tasks.
In that way they are an important foundation for the welfare society.
Local self-government is a form of close-to-the-people democracy, a nærdemokrati.
It gives the individual citizen the opportunity to influence the conditions that are close to citizens' everyday lives.
That can be in the municipality or in the region.
It happens, among other things, through municipal and regional elections.
Alongside national democracy in the Folketing there is thus also local and regional democracy in the country's municipalities and regions.
The municipalities' right to manage their own affairs independently is in the constitution.
But there is not much else in it about the municipalities, and nothing about which tasks they should solve.
It is the Folketing that sets the framework for local self-government and decides the municipalities' tasks.
The state supervises how the municipalities solve their tasks.
The idea behind local self-government is that public tasks that affect individual citizens' daily lives should be solved as close to the citizens as possible.
This is often called the proximity principle, nærhedsprincippet.
There is also a tradition that municipalities, as far as possible, should themselves be able to decide how they will solve and finance the local tasks.
Often the municipalities get the chance to solve public tasks in the way that best suits local needs and wishes.
Municipalities also have the right to levy tax.
In that way they themselves help to raise most of the money to solve their tasks.
But there is a big difference between the populations living in the individual municipalities.
Some municipalities have many more citizens with high incomes than others, and thus a better tax base.
Other municipalities have more citizens on transfer income, for example cash benefit, unemployment benefit or early retirement pension, and thus higher expenses.

To make sure there is money for a reasonably uniform welfare society all over Denmark, there is therefore a series of municipal equalisation schemes and state grants that move a lot of money between the municipalities.
Besides this, it is the Folketing and the government that set the conditions for the municipalities' work.
And the relationship between state and municipalities is sometimes marked by conflict.
The Folketing and the government are interested in the municipalities following national policy, and in all municipalities in the country giving citizens roughly the same offers and conditions.
In contrast, some municipalities feel from time to time that the state interferes too much in local self-government.
They think the municipalities are deprived of the opportunity to decide for themselves how they want to solve the tasks.

The state and the municipalities can themselves levy taxes.

The media play an important role for democracy in Denmark in several ways.
On the one hand, radio, TV, newspapers, magazines and social media and so on help bring the political debate out to a wider circle of citizens.
On the other hand, the media also function as channels where citizens can contribute to the debate with their opinions.
Finally, the media can themselves influence the political agenda.
In all three ways they act as a link between politicians and voters.
The Danish media are independent of the government.
They can therefore freely debate and take a critical view of the political agenda.
Earlier, a number of Danish newspapers functioned as mouthpieces for the political parties.
They were, in other words, controlled by party politics.
Even in many smaller towns, four newspapers were published, which represented the four old parties: the Social Democrats, Venstre, the Social Liberal Party and the Conservative People's Party.
The newspapers faithfully reproduced the party's views, and the readers were often members of the party.
During the 1960s, newspapers changed character and freed themselves from the political parties.
Most newspapers do still have political views, which can be centre-right or left-leaning.
But these views are mainly expressed in the newspapers' so-called editorials, which are the newspapers' own comments on political events.
Since the 1980s, newspapers have taken on the task of being "society's watchdog" even more clearly.
That is, they keep an eye on all kinds of holders of power on behalf of citizens.
On most media, a story that is critical of those in power is regarded as a good news story.
That is why people also talk about the media as "the fourth power of the state".

Here the politicians can themselves present or comment on a case instead of appearing for an interview with journalists in newspapers, on radio or on TV.
The population can likewise comment themselves, ask questions, write or share a post about political topics.

On the other hand, debate on social media often takes place without the journalists having the opportunity to ask critical questions.

For example in the local school, where parents and pupils can discuss the school's affairs in the school board, or in class councils and pupil councils.
This democracy in everyday life is also found on the boards of housing associations and cooperative associations.
There is also a long tradition of employees having insight into, and influence on, conditions at their workplace through a so-called cooperation committee, a samarbejdsudvalg.
In all of these contexts, people work according to democratic principles.
Denmark is also characterised by a rich associational and organisational life.
There are not many other countries where people are members of as many associations and organisations.
About 90 percent of the Danish population are members of at least one association, and about 35 percent have done voluntary work through an association.
On average, every Dane is a member of three to four associations or organisations.
They can be organisations on the labour market, or leisure organisations where the members gather around a common hobby or interest such as football, scouting, birdlife, chess or ceramics.
Others are members of organisations that want to promote particular causes, for example protecting the environment, like the Danish Society for Nature Conservation.
For many citizens, association life and everyday democracy also work as a training in democracy.
Here you discuss matters with each other, gather knowledge, test arguments, make compromises and vote on proposals.
Participants in that way become used to trying to find reasonable solutions to the problems they have gathered around.
Life in the associations and democracy in everyday life give citizens, in other words, a practical knowledge of democratic values and principles.
The most widespread democratic activity is voting when there is an election.
You are not obliged to vote, but the vast majority do so anyway, and voter turnout, that is how many of those with the right to vote actually vote, is quite high compared with most other countries.
It is particularly high when there are elections to the Folketing, an average of 86 percent since the year 2000.
It is somewhat lower when voting for municipal and regional elections, an average of 72 percent since 2000, and a bit lower still for the European Parliament, an average of 58 percent since 2000.
The generally high turnout in Denmark can have several explanations.
One of them is that Danes are brought up to democracy as children and young people.
They learn democratic values early, and voting is a crucial democratic value.
This happens, among other places, in the folkeskole and in the youth educations.
Another explanation is that the strong tradition of being part of associations strengthens citizens' democratic values and ability to cope in organisations.
Finally, it may also matter that democracy in Denmark has from the beginning been a popular project.
Democracy was carried forward not least by the farmers and the workers.
They were organised early in the great movements that became the parties Venstre and the Social Democrats.
This has created a tradition of democratic participation that still marks Denmark.
Danes today are generally very satisfied with their democracy.
They have trust in the institutions of democracy, state, region and municipality.
But not necessarily in the elected political leaders.
Trust in the politicians goes up and down.
The population's political participation is high compared with many other countries.
But over a longer period, participation has changed character.
Fewer people today are members of a political party, even though anyone can become a member of one if they want.
And the so-called grassroots movements play a smaller role today than they did in the 1970s and 1980s.
Instead, new ways of expressing political views have been created.
It can be by signing a political declaration, a petition, by giving money to a political or humanitarian cause, or by taking political or ethical considerations as a consumer.
Many also take part in political discussions on social media such as X and Facebook on the internet.

Every democracy has to answer one hard question: how far can the state go?
In a democracy like the Danish one, there are limits to the state's power over the individual citizen.
Citizens have a number of fundamental rights which the state must respect, and which protect them against abuse by the power of the state.
The constitution thus protects a number of freedoms and human rights which the state power, including the Folketing, must respect.

The constitution contains, among other things, protection of freedom of expression, ytringsfrihed, which is the right to freely express your opinions and to freely communicate your thoughts to others.
Freedom of assembly, forsamlingsfrihed, the right to freely gather and together express your views.
And freedom of association, foreningsfrihed, the right to form associations and to be a member of these associations.
Freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and freedom of association are all crucial preconditions for a democracy.
They are called the political freedoms.
If democracy is to function, there must be a free and open debate.
People must have the right to criticise, challenge and ask critical questions to those in power, public institutions or religious authorities.
So in Denmark you cannot demand that other people never criticise your religion.
The limits are set by law, for example defamation, and only the courts decide whether they have been crossed.
Everyone must also have the right to meet with others and to be a member of a political association.
Citizens must together be free to develop and mark common views, whether or not they go against the views of the majority.
In Denmark, these basic freedoms are, as mentioned, protected in the constitution.
This means citizens have the right to express themselves, form associations and hold meetings, without the state having to approve this in advance.
That means the government cannot demand that, for example, books and newspapers must be approved before they are published.
Every freedom is exercised under responsibility.
There are therefore certain limits to the political freedoms.
If you for example exceed the limits of the law for freedom of expression, you can, depending on the circumstances, be punished and sentenced to pay compensation.
This applies, among other things, if you speak about other citizens in a way that violates their honour, defamation.
It also applies if the press exceeds the limits of freedom of expression, for example by writing something offensive, defamatory, about a person.

Likewise, after repeated incidents in which the Koran was burned in public, it has also become forbidden to publicly treat certain religious writings improperly by burning or otherwise destroying them.
An association can also be judged unlawful and demanded dissolved if it seeks to reach its goals by violence or other illegality.
But the limits are wide in Denmark.
It is also part of democracy that only the courts can decide whether the limits for freedom of expression and other rights secured by the constitution have been exceeded.
The constitution also limits the state's possibility to interfere in the individual citizen's private life.
The constitution thus protects personal freedom, the inviolability of the home, and the right of property.
The constitution also has some provisions that secure citizens the right to certain benefits from the public sector.
Children have the right to free education in the folkeskole.
And citizens have the right to certain public help, if they meet certain obligations in the law.
The constitution also contains a few rules that forbid discrimination.
It says in the constitution that no distinction can be made between citizens' rights or duties to fulfil ordinary civic duties on the basis of faith or descent.
When rights appear in the constitution, the Folketing and the government must not legislate in conflict with these rights.
But in the last instance it is up to the independent courts to assess whether that happens.
Citizens' fundamental rights are not only protected by the constitution, but also by rules adopted by the Folketing, and by international conventions which Denmark has joined.
In 1992, the European Convention on Human Rights was made part of Danish legislation.
The Convention on Human Rights supplements and builds out the freedoms and human rights that follow from the constitution.
The courts can take a stand on whether Danish authorities comply with the convention's requirements.
Denmark can be convicted at the European Court of Human Rights if the country's laws and decisions conflict with the convention's requirements.

In 1994, Denmark was convicted at the European Court of Human Rights in a case where a journalist had been sentenced for passing on racist statements.
This happened because he had made a TV item where he interviewed people who made racist statements.
The Court of Human Rights established that the Danish judgment was in conflict with his freedom of expression as a journalist.
The public administration, the state authorities, regions and municipalities, has the task of putting the country's laws into effect.
The public administration must, among other things, make the welfare society's offers available to citizens.
It is also the public administration that collects taxes and duties.
In an international context, the public administration in Denmark is characterised by being very little corrupt.
The public administration must obey the country's laws when it carries out its tasks.
This applies to authorities in the state, regions and municipalities.
The public administration cannot act on its own.
It is said that the administration's actions must have a legal basis, hjemmel, in a law.
The administration must not act in conflict with the laws.
According to the constitution, it is the independent courts that control the public administration.
At the same time, the state must supervise the municipalities.
Citizens can also in certain areas complain to a board if they for example think that their municipality has not complied with the rules of the law.
In the Danish constitution it is also laid down that the administration is controlled by the Parliamentary Ombudsman, Folketingets Ombudsmand.
The Ombudsman assesses whether errors or neglect have occurred in the public authorities' work.

The Ombudsman must help ensure that the public authorities do not do anything illegal, and that they treat citizens in accordance with the applicable legislation and give them the rights they are entitled to.
The Ombudsman is elected by the Folketing, but is independent in their work.
Neither the Folketing, the government nor the public authorities can interfere in the Ombudsman's work.
The Ombudsman cannot overrule a public authority's decision.
But the Ombudsman can criticise and urge the authorities to change practice, and the Ombudsman's written statements therefore still have great importance for the administration's behaviour.
Openness is often emphasised as one of the most important preconditions of democracy.
The individual citizen must be able to get information about the state and its handling of cases.
The legislative, the judicial and the executive power are all subject to rules about openness.
The Folketing: the meetings are public, so anyone can come and attend the meetings in the chamber.
This is directly in the constitution.
Recordings from the meetings can also be seen on the Folketing's website.
The courts: citizens are allowed to attend all trials.
And the media must be free to inform the population about what happens in trials.
The courts can, however, decide that a trial must be held behind closed doors.
Then neither citizens nor journalists have access to the courtroom.
That can for example be out of consideration for clearing up the case, or for the safety of witnesses, or if the cases concern the security of the state.
The public administration: citizens have, as a starting point, the right to gain insight into the work of the public administration.
It follows from the Public Administration Act, forvaltningsloven, that a party to a case has the right to access to the case's documents, aktindsigt.
Every citizen normally also has the right to know the information which the public administration holds about them.
The Access to Public Administration Files Act, offentlighedsloven, also lays down that anyone, under certain conditions, has the right to see the documents an authority holds.
This applies regardless of whether the documents concern oneself.
But there are some conditions and limits to this right, which after a weighing can mean that other considerations weigh more than the right to access in the specific case.
For example, the right to access normally does not include private information.

All men and women with Danish citizenship over 18 years of age who have residence or stay in Denmark must serve conscription for a period.
In practice, there is no need for all young people in an age group to serve their conscription.
If there are not enough volunteers, it is decided by lottery whether you must serve conscription.
If you fail to turn up for the service you are ordered to do, you can be punished with imprisonment.
If the outcome of the lottery is that you do not have to serve conscription, you have drawn a so-called free number, a frinummer.
Until the first of July, 2025, only men had conscription, and women could decide for themselves whether they wanted to serve, if they were declared suitable for it.
Conscription can be served in the Army, the Navy, the Air Force and the Danish Emergency Management Agency, and the service lasts eleven months.
The length of service has also varied through history.
In the period 2005 to 26, most conscripts served for four months.
As part of the wish to strengthen Danish defence, conscripts from February 2026 must, as a starting point, serve for 11 months.
If you for reasons of conscience do not wish to serve your conscription in the defence or the rescue service, you can become a conscientious objector, a militærnægter.
A conscientious objector can serve their conscription by doing other work for the benefit of society.
That can for example be in institutions for children, young people and the elderly, or in cultural institutions such as museums and theatres.
Second, civic office, borgerligt ombud, or just an ombud.
An ombud is a task, a hverv, which society can impose on a citizen.
Anyone who is appointed to such a task must accept it.
It can for example be sitting on a municipal council, if the citizen is elected, or serving as a lay judge, lægdommer, a juror or nævning, at a court.
Lay judges are ordinary people who help to judge in a criminal case.
They must both assess whether the accused person is guilty, and help decide what the punishment should be.
Anyone can apply to become a lay judge.
If a citizen does not obey the law, they can often be punished.
It does, however, require that it directly appears from a law that the crime can be punished.
The most serious crimes are contained in the Criminal Code, straffeloven.
It has, among other things, provisions about sexual offences, crimes against life and limb, that is homicide and violence, and crimes of enrichment, theft and so on.
In Denmark, the age of criminal responsibility is 15 years.
That means children and young people under 15 cannot be punished for a crime.
This is because they are assessed as immature and unable to assess the consequences of their actions.
Children aged 10 to 14 who commit crimes can instead of punishment, for example, be ordered to do community service, to clean up after vandalism, or to be at home in a specific period of time.
The child can also be placed in a closed institution.
Cases about children aged 10 to 14 are handled by a special Youth Crime Board, Ungdomskriminalitetsnævn.
The usual punishments are fines and imprisonment.
Foreigners can also be sentenced to expulsion from Denmark if they commit crimes.
In the case of very serious crimes such as terrorism, Danish citizens can by a court judgment be deprived of their Danish citizenship.
A citizenship cannot, however, be taken away from a person if they would become stateless.
The death penalty cannot be imposed in Denmark.
The last executions in Denmark took place in the period 1945 to 50.
In total, 78 persons were sentenced to death for having helped the German occupying power during the war.
46 of the 78 death sentences were carried out.
The last execution for a crime committed in peacetime took place in 1892.
Finally, criminal cases and the police.
It is not the courts themselves, but only the prosecution service, anklagemyndigheden, that can bring a criminal case.
This follows from the Administration of Justice Act, retsplejeloven.
Certain less serious criminal cases must be brought by private persons, most often the one who is the victim of the crime.
This applies, for example, to cases about breaches of the peace and defamation.
The prosecution service is the public authority that on behalf of society decides whether charges are to be brought, and thereby whether a criminal case is to be brought before the courts at all.
After that, the courts decide whether the citizen is guilty and is to be punished.
A long series of smaller cases can be settled without the involvement of the courts by the offender accepting to pay a fine.
This is for example the case with many violations of the road traffic act.
If the fine is not paid, the case is brought before the courts.
The prosecution service is subject to the Ministry of Justice, which is led by the Minister of Justice.

The prosecution service consists of the Director of Public Prosecutions, the Rigsadvokat, who is the top leader of the prosecution service, as well as three state prosecutors and the chief constables.
The police are part of the state administration.
That means the state has overall responsibility for the police.
The prosecution service must convince the judges that the accused is guilty.
Every reasonable doubt must benefit the accused.
The police must through investigation obtain the necessary evidence.
If you want to report a crime, it must be reported to the police.
You do not normally have a duty to report a crime to the police.
Both police and prosecution service have a duty to be objective and ensure that it is the right persons who are punished, and that innocent people are not prosecuted.
It is the police who investigate criminal matters, but the courts control the lawfulness of the investigation the police carry out.
The Administration of Justice Act has rules about which interventions the police can make against a citizen when they investigate a case.
This can for example be searching a citizen's property.
The police must not use force during interrogation.
They cannot therefore force a person to give a statement.
Everyone is, however, obliged to give name, address and date of birth to the police.
If a citizen wants to complain about the behaviour of the police, a complaint can be made to the Independent Police Complaints Authority, Den Uafhængige Politiklagemyndighed.
The police can under certain conditions arrest a person who is reasonably suspected of a punishable offence.
If a citizen is arrested, they must be brought before a judge within 24 hours, one døgn.
It is up to the judge to decide whether the citizen is to be released or remanded in custody while the police and the prosecution service investigate the case.
The judge can also choose to maintain the arrest for three times 24 hours, but that is only how long the arrest may be maintained afterwards.
